How to speak in a lower voice

A low voice starts with relaxation, not with pushing your larynx down. Breathe into your belly, say “mmm” on your lowest comfortable note and feel the vibration in your chest. Speak from there, calmly and without forcing.
Don’t fake a bass – your throat will tire. Yawn gently to open your throat and speak on the out-breath, a little slower than usual. Depth comes by itself once you stop rushing.

Put your hand on your breastbone and say “mmmaaa” low and soft. If you feel a tremor under your fingers, that’s your chest resonance. Practise it for two minutes a day and carry that feeling into ordinary sentences.

Breathe from your diaphragm: hand under your ribs, breathe in through your nose so your belly rises, not your shoulders. Then a long exhale on “sss” for twenty seconds. That’s the fuel for a warm, steady voice.
Shoulders down, belly relaxed. Breathe in for four, hold for two, breathe out for six. When your breath is calm, your voice sounds confident and low too.

Hoarseness usually means your vocal folds are tired or dry. Sip water, inhale steam and give your voice a day of silence – but don’t whisper, whispering tires it too. If it lasts longer than two weeks, see a voice doctor – that matters.

My favourite warm-up: three minutes of humming on “mmm”, then lip trills like a little horse, and finally a glide from a high to a low note on “ooo”. Five minutes and your voice is warm and ready for anything.
Start by yawning with an open throat, then “brrr” on your lips and a slow “ma-me-mi-mo-mu” at a medium pitch. A warmed-up voice sounds lower and fuller.
Speak slower than you think you need to. A slow pace sounds confident and warm; a fast one sounds nervous. Try reading a paragraph at half speed and record yourself – you’ll hear the difference.
A pause is your secret weapon. Stop for a second before an important word and everyone will wait for it. Silence in a conversation isn’t emptiness – it’s tension that you control.
Bring a flat voice to life with melody: slightly up when something pleases you, lower and softer when you want to draw someone in. Smile while you talk – you really can hear it.
Let your pitch fall at the end of a statement. When you go up, you sound as if you’re asking for permission. Falling intonation sounds calm and confident.

Confidence is heard before it’s seen. Stand straight, take a calm breath into your belly and speak a little slower and lower than usual. Don’t end sentences with a questioning tone, even when you’re nervous.
Stress before a conversation – a one-minute plan
Before an important conversation, take three long exhales and say one sentence you know well out loud. Your body calms down, and your voice follows your body.
You shape timbre with resonance: more chest gives warmth, more of the facial “mask” gives brightness. Hum “mmm”, look for vibration in your lips and nose, then speak with the same feeling.
A warm timbre means an open throat and a relaxed jaw. Imagine you have warm tea in your mouth and speak with that space inside.
A warm voice is born from relaxation. Drop your shoulders, relax your tongue and speak a bit more on the out-breath, as if telling a secret to someone close. Yes, just like that.
For diction: hold a cork or a pencil between your teeth and read a text slowly for three minutes. Then take it out and read again – you’ll feel your mouth working more clearly on its own.

The Polish “sz” and “cz” sound natural when the tip of your tongue is slightly raised behind the gum ridge and your lips are gently rounded. Slowly repeat “szczery, szczupły, czuły” and don’t clench your teeth. With my Spanish accent, I practise this too.
Vocal folds love water, sleep and calm. Drink plenty, avoid shouting and throat-clearing – swallow instead. Alcohol and cigarettes dry out the voice, so go easy, mi amor.
Louder doesn’t mean from the throat. Power comes from the belly: imagine sending your voice to the back row while your throat stays loose. Practise short “hey!”s supported by your diaphragm.
A quiet voice can be very magnetic, but don’t whisper without sound – it strains the vocal folds. Speak softly, with breath, but with a little tone inside. That way it’s both gentle and healthy.

Nobody likes their recorded voice, because normally you hear yourself through the bones of your skull. Record yourself regularly for a week and your ear will get used to it. Speak to the mic from a hand’s width away and a little more quietly.
On the phone nobody sees your smile, but they hear it. Smile before you answer, speak slower than in person and leave short pauses so the other person can come in.

When you speak in public, start with a pause and a calm look around the room, and only then say your first sentence, low and slow. Stress important words with silence, not shouting. You have time – the room will wait for you.
When your voice cracks or squeaks
Squeaking and cracking usually come from tension in the larynx. Relax your neck, yawn, then speak on “mmm”, moving into words. Don’t lift your chin – keep it relaxed, parallel to the floor.

A tense jaw kills the warmth of your voice. Massage the muscles near your ears, open your mouth wide and close it slowly a few times. Stand straight, feet hip-width apart, and your voice opens up at once.
A nasal voice – how to open it

If you sound nasal, check that your soft palate lifts: say “ka-ga-ka-ga” and feel the movement at the back of your mouth. Then yawn with your mouth closed – it opens the space and takes away the nasality.

In the morning your vocal folds are still stiff and slightly swollen, so your voice is lower and rough. Drink warm water, hum for two minutes and only then talk for longer. That low morning voice? It can be charming too.
What to drink for a healthy voice
Plain water is best – lots of it, often. Warm tea with honey soothes, but not hot. Milk and very sweet drinks right before speaking cause phlegm, so avoid them.
Don’t keep clearing your throat – it’s like knocking your vocal folds together. Swallow or sip some water instead, and make a gentle “hm” on the out-breath.
My accent? It’s a melody from Spain – open vowels and a soft “r”. If you want to sound more melodic, lengthen the vowels in stressed syllables and don’t be afraid of a sing-song sentence.
A smile lifts your timbre and adds warmth. Say a sentence once with a straight face and once with a slight smile, and record both. The second always sounds friendlier and more pleasant.
Read stories aloud and let emotions change your pace and volume. Sadness slows down, joy speeds up, mystery goes quiet. Your voice is an instrument, mi amor – play it.
Singing is great training for your speaking voice: it teaches breathing, resonance and melody. Start with simple songs in a comfortable, low key and hum them before singing at full voice.
How long it takes to change your voice
You’ll hear the first results after two or three weeks of ten minutes a day. A lasting change in timbre takes a few months. Consistency beats intensity.
Your voice changes throughout life: in puberty, with hormones and with age. Good habits – breathing, hydration and not forcing – will keep it young and warm for a long time.
Humming is the best massage for your vocal folds. Lips closed, teeth apart, tongue loose, and “mmm” at a comfortable pitch. Look for a tickle in your lips – that means the resonance is working.
A warm, deep voice isn’t a bass at any cost – it’s calm and support. Speak from your belly, end sentences going down and don’t apologise with your tone for what you say. That really sounds good.
